g10-geography-ug4-t1.overview: World population has grown more since 1950 than in all previous human existence, and Africa is its fastest-growing continent. This lesson compares the size and share of each region's people, explains why growth accelerated after World War II, and introduces doubling time and the demographic balancing equation.
objectives: Describe the size and regional distribution of world population using population tables
Compare Africa's population size and share with the other continents
Explain why world and African population growth accelerated after World War II
Compute population doubling time using the Rule of 70
Apply the demographic balancing equation to calculate population change in an area
g10-geography-ug4-t1.simple: World population grew slowly for most of history and then exploded after World War II. A billion people were added between 1960 and 1975 and another billion between 1975 and 1987. Humanity entered the twentieth century with 1.6 billion people and left it with 6.1 billion. By mid-2020 the world held more than 7 billion people: Asia was most populous with 59.4 percent, Africa second with 17.5 percent, and Oceania least with only 43 million. Growth is fast because modern medicine and better living standards cut death rates while births stay high. Africa grows fastest of all, about 2.5 percent a year, doubling roughly every 28 years by the Rule of 70. Any population changes through births, deaths and migration, combined in the demographic balancing equation.
g10-geography-ug4-t1.detailed:
A world of growing numbers. World population growth accelerated sharply after World War II, when the population of less developed countries began to increase dramatically. A billion people were added to the world population between 1960 and 1975, and another billion were added between 1975 and 1987. The human population entered the twentieth century with 1.6 billion people and left it with 6.1 billion. In fact, there has been more population growth since 1950 than in all the previous years of human existence.

Where the world's people live. Population growth and distribution differ significantly among the major regions. Between 1970 and 2021 Asia's share of world population rose from 58% to 61%, Africa's rose from 10% to 13%, and Latin America and the Caribbean's rose from 8% to 9%; over the same period Northern America's share slipped to about 5% and Europe's fell from 18% to 12%. By mid-2020 the world had more than 7 billion people. Asia is the most populous continent with about 59.4% of humanity, roughly 4.6 billion people; Africa is second with 17.5%; and Oceania is the least populated continent with only about 43 million people.

Why the world population grows so fast. Over the past seven decades the world has seen enormous changes in fertility and life expectancy. In the early 1970s women had on average 4.5 children each; by 2015 total fertility for the world had fallen below 2.5 children per woman. Average global life expectancy rose from 64.6 years in the early 1990s to 70.8 years in 2020. Growth continues because fertility, although declining, has not fallen at the same pace as mortality. The high growth of recent centuries is largely the result of advances in modern medicine and improvements in living standards, which significantly reduced infant, child and maternal mortality and raised life expectancy.

Africa's size and extraordinary speed. Africa is the world's second most populous continent next to Asia, with more than 1.3 billion people by mid-2020, about 17.5% of the world total. Its population is nearly one-third of Asia's but 32 times that of Oceania. Africa grows fastest of all continents: as of 2018 its growth rate stood at about 2.5% per year, the highest in the world and twice the world average. Sub-Saharan Africa experiences the world's highest rate of natural increase, about 3% per year, and its population is projected to grow from about 700 million in 1995 to 1.6 billion people by 2030, driven by a total fertility rate of about 6.0 children per woman, twice the world average. History shows the contrast with today: Africa's population had been increasing very slowly until recent times, taking more than 700 years to nearly double between 1000 and 1700 AD and another 200 years for that doubling, but since the 1950s it has taken on average only about 25 years to double.

Doubling time and the Rule of 70. Doubling time is the time it takes for a population to double in size, and it is computed with the Rule of 70 by dividing 70 by the growth rate r: dt = 70/r. A population growing at 2.5% a year therefore doubles in 70 divided by 2.5, which is 28 years. The textbook example: Ethiopia, with 110 million people in 2020 and a growth rate of 2.5%, would take 28 years to double to 220 million. Africa's combination of very high fertility and the world's fastest decline in mortality gives the continent the world's shortest doubling time.

What makes a population change. Population change is a function of three variables: fertility (births), mortality (deaths) and migration. Births and deaths combine to form natural increase, the excess of births over deaths, while net migration is the balance of immigrants over emigrants. Population change in an area can be calculated with the demographic balancing equation: Pt - Po = B - D + I - O, where Pt is population at the end of the period, Po at the beginning, B births, D deaths, I in-migration and O out-migration.

Challenges behind the numbers. Africa's massive growth brings interrelated challenges: producing sufficient food, providing health care and adequate education to hundreds of millions of young people, environmental degradation, increasing scarcity of freshwater, and the emigration of millions of Africans out of the continent. The factors behind the growth itself are demographic and socioeconomic: high crude birth rates, high fertility rates, childbirth at a young age, low rates of contraceptive use in most African nations, declines in infant, maternal and overall death rates, rising life expectancy, and declining HIV/AIDS-related deaths.

keyTerms.def: Traits of a population such as its size, growth rate, birth and death rates, age and sex composition.
The time it takes for a population to double in size or value.
A rule for computing doubling time: divide 70 by the growth rate r of the population, so dt = 70/r.
The excess of births over deaths in a population during a period; births minus deaths.
The balance between immigration (coming in) and emigration (going out); immigrants minus emigrants.
The equation for calculating population change from one year to the next: population change = births - deaths + in-migration - out-migration.
The occurrence of births in a population; a natural positive factor that increases population size.
The occurrence of deaths in a population; a natural negative factor that decreases population size.

workedExamples.problem: The population of Ethiopia is 110 million in 2020 with a growth rate of 2.5%. How many years would it take for Ethiopia's population to double?
workedExamples.given: Population size 110 million in 2020; growth rate r = 2.5% per year.
workedExamples.formula: dt = 70 / r, where dt is doubling time and r is the growth rate.
workedExamples.calculation: 70 divided by 2.5 equals 28 years; the doubling time is independent of the starting size of 110 million.
workedExamples.answer: 28 years; Ethiopia's population would double to 220 million by about 2048.

workedExamples.problem: Country Y grows at 1.0% per year while Africa grows at 2.5% per year. Compare their doubling times to explain why Africa has the world's shortest.
workedExamples.given: Country Y growth rate = 1.0%; Africa growth rate = 2.5%.
workedExamples.substitution: Country Y: dt = 70 / 1.0 = 70 years; Africa: dt = 70 / 2.5 = 28 years.
workedExamples.calculation: The higher the growth rate, the shorter the doubling time, so Africa doubles about 2.5 times faster than Country Y.
workedExamples.answer: Country Y needs about 70 years to double; Africa needs only about 28 years, the shortest in the world.

workedExamples.problem: An area began 2020 with 2,000,000 people. During the year it recorded 50,000 births, 30,000 deaths, 10,000 in-migrants and 25,000 out-migrants. Find its end-of-year population.
workedExamples.formula: Pt - Po = B - D + I - O, or Pt - Po = NI + NM.
workedExamples.answer: The end-of-year population is 2,005,000; natural increase added 20,000 people while net out-migration removed 15,000.

commonMistakes: Believing the world population was always large, when in fact humanity entered the twentieth century with only 1.6 billion people.
Confusing the most populous continent (Asia, 59.4%) with the fastest-growing continent (Africa).
Thinking doubling time depends on the size of the population; it depends only on the growth rate.
Counting migration as part of natural increase, when natural increase is only births minus deaths.
Assuming a large population always grows faster than a small one; Oceania is tiny, while less populous regions can grow faster in percentage terms.
Forgetting that emigration explains population loss, not just higher death rates.
applications: Using the Rule of 70 to predict how long Ethiopia's population would take to double at its current growth rate.
Reading the UN World Population Data Sheet tables to compare Africa's share of world population with that of Asia and Europe.
Explaining why schools, clinics and housing face rising demand as Africa's population doubles roughly every 25 years.
Predicting what a doubling of population would mean for farmland, freshwater and jobs in a given region.
Using the balancing equation to explain why a town can grow quickly through in-migration even when its birth rate is moderate.
g10-geography-ug4-t1.summary: World population entered the twentieth century at 1.6 billion and reached about 7.8 billion by 2021, with Asia holding 59.4 percent and Africa 17.5 percent of the total. Growth accelerated after World War II because modern medicine and better living standards cut mortality faster than fertility fell, leaving Africa with the world's highest growth rate of about 2.5 percent a year and the shortest doubling time of roughly 28 years. Any population change equals natural increase (births minus deaths) plus net migration (in-migrants minus out-migrants).

g10-geography-ug4-t2.overview: Africa holds the world's highest fertility and the world's highest infant mortality, yet both death rates and birth rates are falling. This lesson measures those trends with TFR, CBR, CDR, IMR, maternal mortality and life expectancy, and projects them to 2050.
objectives: Define total fertility rate, crude birth rate, crude death rate, infant mortality rate, maternal mortality ratio and life expectancy
Analyze fertility patterns across Africa's regions using rate tables
Explain the causes and recent trends of mortality in Africa
Compare Africa's fertility and mortality levels with other world regions
Interpret projections of Africa's future fertility and mortality
g10-geography-ug4-t2.simple: Fertility means the occurrence of births; mortality means the occurrence of deaths. Africa has the highest fertility in the world: the total fertility rate fell from 6.6 children per woman in 1980 to 4.7 in 2016 and 4.5 in 2017, and the crude birth rate of 33 per 1000 in 2020 tops even other developing regions. Somalia records Africa's highest crude birth rate at 49 per 1000, while Mauritius has the lowest at 11. Mortality is falling quickly: the crude death rate dropped to 8 per 1000 by mid-2020, yet infant mortality at 47 per 1000 live births is the world's largest. Life expectancy averages 64 years, ranging from 59 in Western Africa to 74 in Northern Africa.
g10-geography-ug4-t2.detailed:
Measuring births. Fertility refers to the occurrence of births in the human population, a natural positive factor that increases population size. Demographers use two main measures. The total fertility rate (TFR) is the average number of children a woman would give birth to during her lifetime if she passed through her childbearing years (15-49) experiencing the present-day age-specific fertility rates. The crude birth rate (CBR) is the number of live births per 1000 of the mid-year total population in a given year, computed as CBR = (total annual live births / total mid-year population) x 1000.

Africa's fertility trend. Africa's TFR has steadily declined over the last two decades: it stood at 6.6 children per woman in 1980, was 5.1 in 2004, 4.7 in 2016 and 4.5 in 2017. Yet this remains the highest fertility in the world. The decline has not been uniform across regions. Northern Africa changed little, at 3.4 in 2004 and again in 2016 before slipping to 2.9 by 2020; Central Africa stagnated at around 6 children per woman; while by 2020 Southern Africa was lowest at 2.4, followed by Northern Africa, and Central Africa was highest at 5.8 followed by Western Africa at 5.1, with Eastern Africa at 4.3.

Fertility by crude birth rate. Even by the CBR measure Africa leads the world with 33 births per 1000 population in 2020, well above the average of 20 per 1000 for less developed countries. Variation within the continent is huge: in Eastern Africa itself, Somalia had the continent's highest CBR at 49/1000 while Mauritius had the lowest at 11/1000. Other notable values include Niger and Chad at 47/1000, Ethiopia at 32/1000, South Africa at 19/1000 and Tunisia at 16/1000. High fertility persists because of less access to contraceptives, high poverty, the low status of women, the need for many children for the labor force, children seen as a symbol of virility, low educational background, early marriage and the influence of traditions and cultures on family size.

Future fertility. In projections to 2050, the African population is expected to peak at 2.5 billion, up from 1.0 billion in 2010, which would represent 25% of the world's population. Lower fertility is expected to bring Africa's annual population growth rate down to about 2% by 2030, compared with Asia at 1.0%, Latin America and the Caribbean at 1.2%, Eastern Europe at -0.8% and the world as a whole at 1.5%. Northern Africa is the exception within the continent, with growth expected to decline to about 0.8% a year by 2030.

Measuring deaths. Mortality refers to the occurrence of death in the human population, a negative factor that decreases population size. Its measures are the crude death rate (CDR), deaths per 1000 of the mid-year population; the infant mortality rate (IMR), deaths of infants before their first birthday per 1000 live births, the most widely used indicator of a country's general health situation; the maternal mortality ratio (MMR), maternal deaths per 100,000 live births; and life expectancy, the average number of years a newborn can expect to live under current mortality levels.

Africa's mortality trend. Deaths in Africa fell from an average of 14 per 1000 population in 2007 to 10 per 1000 in 2016, and stood at 8 per 1000 by mid-2020, close to the world figure of 8; regionally the rate ranges from 6/1000 in Northern and Eastern Africa to 11/1000 in Southern Africa. The continent still has the world's largest infant mortality rate at 47 deaths per 1000 live births: Central Africa is highest at 62/1000, followed by Western Africa at 55/1000 and Sub-Saharan Africa at 50/1000, while Northern Africa is lowest at 22/1000. High mortality persists because of low standard of living, low access to health facilities, poor sanitary practices, civil war and political instability, widespread famine caused by recurrent drought, poor nutrition and high incidence of disease. Progress is expected: child mortality is projected to decline from 116 per 1000 live births in 2010 to 75 per 1000 in 2030, helped by better incomes, improved water supply and sanitation, better health facilities and reduced impact of HIV/AIDS, although malaria remains endemic in most African countries.

Life expectancy. Africa's average life expectancy at birth was 64 years by mid-2020, below the world figure of 73. Regional values differ sharply: Northern Africa reached 74 years and Eastern Africa 66, but Western Africa stood at only 59 years while Central and Southern Africa and Sub-Saharan Africa average 61-62. Almost all sub-Saharan countries have more than 40% of their population under 15, which produces a high dependency ratio. With reduced mortality Africa should expect and plan for an ageing population; by 2030 average life expectancy is projected to surpass 64 years.

keyTerms.def: The occurrence of births in the human population; a natural positive factor that increases population size.
The average number of children a woman would bear during her lifetime if she experienced present-day age-specific fertility rates through ages 15-49.
The number of live births per 1000 of the mid-year total population in a given area and year.
The occurrence of deaths in the human population; a natural negative factor that decreases population size.
The number of deaths occurring per 1000 of the mid-year total population in a given area and year.
The death of infants before their first birthday, measured as annual infant deaths per 1000 live births; the most widely used indicator of general health.
The number of maternal deaths during pregnancy, childbirth or within 42 days of termination of pregnancy, per 100,000 live births.
The average number of years a newborn infant can be expected to live under current mortality levels.

workedExamples.problem: Hypothetical African country X had 2,407,500 live births in 2020 and a mid-year population of 53,500,000. Calculate the country's crude birth rate.
workedExamples.calculation: 2,407,500 divided by 53,500,000 equals 0.045, and 0.045 x 1000 equals 45.
workedExamples.answer: Country X had 45 births per 1000 of the mid-year population in 2020.

workedExamples.problem: Country X recorded 856,000 deaths in 2020 and had a mid-year population of 53,500,000. Calculate the crude death rate.
workedExamples.calculation: 856,000 divided by 53,500,000 equals 0.016, and 0.016 x 1000 equals 16.
workedExamples.answer: Country X had 16 deaths per 1000 of the mid-year population in 2020.

workedExamples.problem: Country Y recorded 12,000 infant deaths and 250,000 live births in 2020. Calculate the infant mortality rate.
workedExamples.formula: IMR = (total annual infant deaths / total annual live births) x 1000.
workedExamples.calculation: 12,000 divided by 250,000 equals 0.048, and 0.048 x 1000 equals 48.
workedExamples.answer: Country Y had about 48 infant deaths per 1000 live births, close to Africa's continental average of 47 in 2020.

workedExamples.problem: Country Z had 10,000 maternal deaths and 3,500,000 live births in 2020. Calculate the maternal mortality ratio.
workedExamples.formula: MMR = (deaths due to maternal causes / total annual live births) x 100,000.
workedExamples.calculation: 10,000 divided by 3,500,000 equals about 0.002857, and 0.002857 x 100,000 equals about 286.
workedExamples.answer: Country Z had about 286 maternal deaths per 100,000 live births in 2020.

commonMistakes: Confusing total fertility rate (children per woman in a lifetime) with crude birth rate (births per 1000 population in a year).
Confusing infant mortality rate, which uses live births as the base, with crude death rate, which uses the total population.
Assuming fertility is the same everywhere in Africa, when Southern Africa's TFR of 2.4 differs sharply from Central Africa's 5.8.
Believing Africa's death rate is rising, when it actually fell from 14 per 1000 in 2007 to 8 per 1000 by mid-2020.
Thinking maternal mortality means deaths of mothers from old age, when it refers to deaths related to pregnancy and childbirth.
Confusing life expectancy with the maximum age a person can reach; it is an average expected figure.
applications: Comparing Ethiopia's crude birth rate of 32 per 1000 with Somalia's 49 and Mauritius' 11 to see internal variation in fertility.
Using infant mortality as the key health indicator to argue for investment in clinics, sanitation and nutrition.
Planning services against the projection that Africa will hold about 2.5 billion people, one quarter of humanity, by 2050.
Explaining why Northern Africa achieved the continent's highest life expectancy of 74 years while Western Africa trails at 59.
Discussing how education for girls and better access to family planning can lower fertility in high-fertility regions.
g10-geography-ug4-t2.summary: Africa has the world's highest fertility: total fertility fell from 6.6 children per woman in 1980 to 4.5 in 2017, and the crude birth rate of 33 per 1000 in 2020 is the global peak, with Somalia highest at 49 and Mauritius lowest at 11. Mortality is falling, with a crude death rate of 8 per 1000 by mid-2020, but infant mortality remains the world's largest at 47 per 1000 live births. Life expectancy averages 64 years, lowest in Western Africa at 59 and highest in Northern Africa at 74, and the population is projected to reach about 2.5 billion by 2050.

g10-geography-ug4-t3.overview: Population structure describes a population by age and sex. Africa's structure is exceptionally young: a median age of 19.7 years, a triangular expansive pyramid, and an age dependency ratio of 78.6 dependents per 100 workers.
objectives: Describe Africa's age structure using the young, working and old age groups
Interpret median age as an indicator of how young or old a population is
Calculate the age dependency ratio and the sex ratio
Read and classify population pyramids as expansive, stationary or constructive
Explain how a young age structure pressures resources and services
g10-geography-ug4-t3.simple: Population structure is the composition of a population by age and sex. Africa is dominated by young people: 41 percent are aged 0-14, 56 percent are 15-64 and only 3 percent are 65 or older, with a median age of just 19.7 years compared with 42.5 in Europe. The age dependency ratio is 78.6 for Africa, meaning roughly 79 dependents for every 100 working-age people; it is highest in Central Africa and lowest in Southern Africa. The sex ratio compares the number of males per 100 females. A population pyramid graphs this structure, with male bars on the left of the central axis and female bars on the right. Africa's pyramid is expansive, triangular, with a broad base caused by high fertility and a tapering apex caused by low life expectancy.
g10-geography-ug4-t3.detailed:
A young continent. The age structure of a population can be expressed by its distribution into young, working and old age groups. Africa is characterized by the dominance of young age population: 41% of its people are aged 0-14, 56% are of working age (15-64) and only 3% are 65 or older. The median age confirms this; Africa's median age was 19.7 years by mid-2020, whereas Europe's was 42.5 years. A low median age implies a young population driven by high fertility and high growth, while a high median age prevails where growth is low and slow.

Regional contrasts. The regional table shows Central Africa with the largest young share at 46% and the highest age dependency ratio at 96.1, followed by Western Africa at 44% young and an ADR of 88.7. Southern Africa stands apart with only 29% young and 6% old, the continent's lowest ADR at 53.8, while Sub-Saharan Africa averages 43% young and an ADR of 85.2. Northern Africa, with 33% young and 5% old, has an ADR of 61.3.

What a young structure costs. In developing continents like Africa the level of fertility is very high and so is population growth. As high fertility persists, pressure on scarce resources for development increases: demand rises for food, education, health facilities, employment opportunities, housing and other services. Physical and institutional infrastructures must be expanded abundantly to meet the growing population's needs, and the persisting high rate of growth constantly dwarfs whatever is achieved in the economic sector. Resources that could serve development are shifted instead to providing basic supplies for additional members.

Sex structure. The sex structure is expressed using the sex ratio, the proportion of males to females: Sex Ratio = (number of males / number of females) x 100, giving males for every 100 females. The textbook example gives a country with 3.6 million males and 4 million females a sex ratio of 90, meaning 90 males per 100 females. The balance of the two sexes affects other demographic elements such as marriage rate, fertility, occupational structure and growth.

The population pyramid. A population pyramid graphically depicts the age-sex composition of a population, showing single years or, most commonly, 5-year age groups. Bars are stacked horizontally in ascending age order: males on the left of the central vertical axis and females on the right. Length represents numbers, and all bars must have the same class interval and equal thickness. Three types are identified: the expansive pyramid has a broad base, indicating a high proportion of children, rapid growth, high birth and death rates and short life expectancy, the typical pattern of less developed countries with poor access to birth control and health care; the constructive pyramid shows fewer young people and a large elderly population, with ages 1-14 below 30% and ages 75+ above 6%, an aging population typical of developed countries with adequate health services; and the stationary pyramid shows fertility and mortality in balance, B = D, with zero population growth.

Characteristics of Africa's population. The textbook summarizes Africa's demography as: high fertility and mortality rates; a generally young population; a triangular, broad-based and tapering population pyramid; high age dependency and youth dependency ratios with a low old dependency ratio; low life expectancy; and a high population growth rate. Most developing countries share the expansive, almost triangular pyramid whose broad base reflects high fertility and whose narrow apex reflects short life expectancy.

keyTerms.def: The composition of a population, especially by age and sex.
The distribution of a population into young (0-14), working (15-64) and old (65+) age groups.
The age that divides a population into two equal halves; a low median age indicates a young population.
The number of dependents (young 0-14 plus old 65+) per 100 people of working age (15-64).
The number of males for every 100 females, computed as (males / females) x 100.
A graph depicting the age-sex composition of a population with horizontal bars: males on the left of the central axis, females on the right.
A pyramid with a broad base indicating a high proportion of children, high birth and death rates, rapid growth and short life expectancy.
An aging population pyramid with under 30% aged 1-14 and over 6% aged 75+, typical of developed countries.

workedExamples.problem: A hypothetical country has a population of 3.6 million males and 4.0 million females. Find its sex ratio.
workedExamples.given: Number of males = 3.6 million; number of females = 4.0 million.
workedExamples.formula: Sex Ratio = (number of males / number of females) x 100.
workedExamples.calculation: 3,600,000 divided by 4,000,000 equals 0.9, and 0.9 x 100 equals 90.
workedExamples.answer: The sex ratio is 90, meaning there are 90 males for every 100 females.

workedExamples.problem: Using Africa's 2020 age shares (41% aged 0-14, 56% aged 15-64, 3% aged 65+), calculate the age dependency ratio.
workedExamples.calculation: 44 divided by 56 equals about 0.786, and multiplying by 100 gives about 78.6.
workedExamples.answer: Africa's ADR is 78.6: about 79 dependents for every 100 working-age people, matching the textbook table.

workedExamples.problem: Central Africa has 46% children, 51% working age and 3% old people. Calculate its ADR and compare it with Africa's average.
workedExamples.calculation: 49 divided by 51 equals about 0.961, so the ADR is about 96.1.
workedExamples.answer: Central Africa's ADR is about 96.1, the highest in the table and well above Africa's average of 78.6.

commonMistakes: Reading a pyramid's base width as a measure of death rates; the broad base shows high fertility and many children.
Placing male bars on the right of the pyramid's axis; males belong on the left and females on the right.
Reversing the sex ratio and reporting females per 100 males instead of males per 100 females.
Confusing the dependency ratio with the percentage of dependents in the total population; the ADR is expressed per 100 workers.
Assuming Africa has a large old-age population, when only about 3% of Africans are 65 or older.
Believing a young population is cost free, ignoring rising demand for food, schools, health care, housing and jobs.
Treating all population pyramids as the same shape, when expansive, constructive and stationary types differ sharply.
applications: Reading a national population pyramid to decide how many classrooms and teachers a country must provide in coming years.
Using the age dependency ratio to argue for investment in jobs so the working population can support dependents.
Comparing Africa's median age of 19.7 with Europe's 42.5 to explain why the two continents face different problems.
Planning child-focused health services where the young share is high and elder care where the old share is growing.
Interpreting an expansive pyramid from a developing country to predict continued rapid population growth.
g10-geography-ug4-t3.summary: Africa's population structure is dominated by the young: 41% are under 15, 56% are of working age and only 3% are 65 or older, giving a median age of 19.7 and an age dependency ratio of 78.6, highest in Central Africa at 96.1. Its expansive, triangular population pyramid reflects high fertility, high mortality, rapid growth and low life expectancy. High fertility keeps pressure on food, education, health, housing and jobs, so growth continually outpaces economic achievement.

g10-geography-ug4-t4.overview: People do not spread evenly across the continent. This lesson distinguishes population distribution from density, locates Africa's densest and emptiest places, computes crude density, and explains the physical and human factors behind the unevenness.
objectives: Define population distribution and population density
Locate the most densely and least densely populated areas of Africa
Compute crude population density from population and area data
Identify the physical and human factors behind Africa's spatial variation
Compare regional population densities using tables and maps
g10-geography-ug4-t4.simple: Population distribution is the way people inhabit and occupy the earth's surface, and Africa's is very uneven. The vast Sahara has few permanent residents, while the Nile Valley of Egypt, Mauritius, Rwanda and Burundi rank among the world's most densely populated areas. Africa's average crude density in mid-2019 was about 44 people per square kilometre, but regional values range from 65 persons/km2 in Eastern and Western Africa down to 25 in Southern Africa. Physical factors such as climate, relief, availability of water, soil fertility and minerals, together with human factors like economic conditions and political situations, determine where people live. The most populous countries are Nigeria, Ethiopia, Egypt, DRC and South Africa; the most densely populated are Mauritius, Rwanda, Burundi, Comoros and Seychelles.
g10-geography-ug4-t4.detailed:
Distribution versus density. Population distribution refers to the way people inhabit and occupy the earth's surface. As elsewhere in the world, Africa's population distribution is uneven, producing areas of high and low density. Population density expresses the same idea numerically: the average number of people per unit of land, usually per square kilometre, computed as crude density = total population / total area. The continent's average crude density in mid-2019 was about 44 people/km2.

Dense and empty Africa. Some parts of the continent, particularly the vast Sahara, have few permanent residents, because desert climate and lack of water make permanent settlement difficult. Other areas rank among the world's most densely populated: the Nile Valley of Egypt, Mauritius, Rwanda and Burundi. Water, fertile soil and favorable climates attract dense settlement, so river valleys and fertile highlands contrast sharply with the surrounding dry lands.

Factors behind the pattern. Certain human and physical factors explain the spatial variation. Among the physical factors are climate, relief, availability of water, fertility of the soil and the distribution of minerals. The human factors that determine how far people inhabit a place include economic conditions, political situations and other social factors. A fertile, well-watered region may still stay sparsely settled if instability or poverty discourages occupation of the land.

Regional densities. Regional variation is significant. Eastern and Western Africa share the continent's highest crude density at 65 persons/km2, followed by Sub-Saharan Africa with 49. Southern Africa is lowest at 25 persons/km2, with Central Africa at 27 and Northern Africa at 31, all below the continental average of 44. These figures let geographers compare the pressure of people on land across regions.

Populous is not the same as dense. At country level, the most populous countries are Nigeria, Ethiopia, Egypt, the Democratic Republic of the Congo and the Republic of South Africa. Yet being populous does not necessarily mean being densely populated. The most densely populated countries are Mauritius, Rwanda, Burundi, Comoros and Seychelles, small countries whose limited land area concentrates their people. A large country can hold many millions of people and still have a low average density, as its big area spreads the population out.

keyTerms.def: The way people inhabit and occupy the earth's surface.
The average number of people per unit of land area, usually per square kilometre.
Total population divided by total area in square kilometres, giving persons per km2.
Differences in a pattern, such as density, from place to place across space.
Natural conditions such as climate, relief, water availability, soil fertility and minerals that shape settlement.
Conditions such as economic conditions, political situations and social factors that shape where people live.

workedExamples.problem: A hypothetical African country has a population of 45 million people on a land area of 900,000 km2. Compute its crude population density and compare it with Africa's average.
workedExamples.formula: Crude density = total population / total area (persons per km2).
workedExamples.calculation: 45,000,000 divided by 900,000 equals 50 persons per km2.
workedExamples.answer: 50 persons/km2, slightly above Africa's continental average of about 44 in mid-2019.

workedExamples.problem: Using the textbook table, compare the crude density of Eastern Africa (65 persons/km2) with that of Southern Africa (25 persons/km2).
workedExamples.given: Eastern Africa 65 persons/km2; Southern Africa 25 persons/km2.
workedExamples.formula: Ratio = density of Eastern Africa / density of Southern Africa.
workedExamples.answer: Eastern Africa is about 2.6 times as densely populated as Southern Africa.

workedExamples.problem: A region of 20,000 km2 has a crude density the same as Eastern Africa's 65 persons/km2. Estimate its population.
workedExamples.answer: About 1.3 million people live in the region.

commonMistakes: Confusing total population size with density; Nigeria is populous while Mauritius is dense.
Forgetting the unit persons per km2 and reporting density as a bare number.
Assuming Africa's population is spread evenly across the continent.
Citing only climate and ignoring human factors such as economics and politics when explaining distribution.
Believing a high average density means people are spread evenly within the region; clustering like the Nile Valley hides empty desert.
Dividing area by population instead of population by area when computing density.
applications: Explaining why dry lowlands of Ethiopia hold few people while fertile, well-watered highlands are crowded.
Using density figures to plan how many schools, clinics and wells a region needs.
Interpreting why the Sahara and other deserts remain almost uninhabited while the Nile Valley supports dense settlement.
Discussing how political instability can empty a fertile area and push people towards denser, safer places.
Using regional density tables to argue which regions need more infrastructure per person on the land.
g10-geography-ug4-t4.summary: Africa's population distribution is uneven: the vast Sahara is nearly empty while the Nile Valley of Egypt, Mauritius, Rwanda and Burundi are among the world's densest areas. The continent averaged about 44 persons/km2 in mid-2019, from a high of 65 in Eastern and Western Africa to a low of 25 in Southern Africa. Physical factors such as climate, relief, water and soil fertility, together with human factors like economics and politics, explain the pattern; populous countries such as Nigeria and Ethiopia are not necessarily the densest.

g10-geography-ug4-t5.overview: Africa's urbanization shows stark contrasts: Gabon is almost 90% urban while Burundi is only 12%. This lesson maps the most and least urbanized countries and regions, explains rural-urban migration, and weighs the costs of uncontrolled urban growth.
objectives: Describe the stark contrasts in urbanization between African countries
Identify the most and least urbanized countries and regions of Africa
Explain the causes and development challenges of rapid urban growth
Interpret the share of urban population by region using tables
Assess the effects of rapid urbanization on rural areas and agriculture
g10-geography-ug4-t5.simple: Urbanization means the rising share of people living in urban areas, and Africa offers stark contrasts. Burundi is the least urbanized country at only 12 percent, and Rwanda, Malawi, Ethiopia, Kenya, Eritrea, Chad, Niger, Uganda and South Sudan also stay mostly rural, while Gabon has almost 90 percent urban and Western Sahara, Libya and Djibouti also rank high. Southern Africa is the most urbanized region at 62 percent and Eastern Africa the least at 26. Today about 41 percent of Africans live in urban areas, and the urban population is projected to exceed the rural population in about two decades. Urban growth, fed by migration from rural areas, strains land, infrastructure and basic services, and uncontrolled urbanization depopulates rural areas and cripples agricultural production.
g10-geography-ug4-t5.detailed:
Stark contrasts. Africa offers stark contrasts in urbanization compared with other world regions. Burundi, Rwanda, Malawi, Ethiopia and Burkina Faso are still predominantly rural, while in Gabon and Western Sahara more than 80% of the population lives in urban areas. Most strikingly, Gabon has almost 90% of its people in towns and cities, whereas Burundi, the least urbanized country on the continent, stands at only 12%.

The top and the bottom. The top 20 countries in urbanization have at least half their population in urban areas. Besides Gabon they include Western Sahara, Libya, Djibouti, Algeria, Tunisia, Sao Tome and Principe, Cape Verde, Congo, South Africa, Angola, Morocco, Gambia, Mauritania, Botswana, Seychelles, Cameroon, Cote D'Ivoire, Ghana and Liberia. The bottom 10 have less than a quarter of their people in towns: Kenya, Eritrea, Chad, Niger, Swaziland, Ethiopia, Uganda and South Sudan, with Malawi and Burundi at the foot of the list. Generally, countries in Northern and Western Africa are more urbanized than those of Eastern Africa.

Regional shares. Eastern Africa is the least urbanized region while Southern Africa is the most urbanized. In 2016 the share of urban population stood at 62% in Southern Africa, 51% in Northern Africa, 47% in Central Africa, 45% in Western Africa and only 26% in Eastern Africa. Continent-wide, urban dwellers are currently about 41% of the total, and the urban population is projected to overtake the rural population in about two decades.

Why cities grow and what it costs. African urban growth reflects sizeable migration flows from rural areas in search of work, services and opportunity. The migrants need access to land, infrastructure and basic services, which presents major challenges for development; the influx has also stretched health care services. Cities that cannot keep pace with arrivals grow crowded, underserved and poor.

The rural cost of urban growth. The unit summary stresses that Africa's rate of urbanization is the highest in the world, but uncontrolled and rapid urbanization has depopulated rural areas. Rural depopulation has crippled agricultural production, especially the production of food crops, and rapid urban growth has become a major cause of growing poverty both in rural and in urban areas.

keyTerms.def: Settlement in the countryside, characteristic of countries where most people live outside towns and cities.
Relating to towns and cities where population is concentrated and non-farm activities dominate.
The increasing share of a population living in urban areas, often driven by rural-urban migration.
The movement of people from the countryside into towns and cities, a major driver of African urban growth.
The percentage of a region's population living in urban areas, as reported for 2016 in the textbook.
The loss of people from rural areas, which uncontrolled rapid urbanization has caused across Africa.

workedExamples.problem: A country has 12 million people and 51% of them live in urban areas. Find its urban and rural population.
workedExamples.formula: Urban population = total population x percentage urban / 100.
workedExamples.answer: About 6.12 million people are urban and 5.88 million rural, mirroring Northern Africa's 51% urban share.

workedExamples.problem: Compare the urbanized character of Southern Africa (62% urban) with Eastern Africa (26% urban) using their 2016 shares.
workedExamples.given: Southern Africa 62% urban; Eastern Africa 26% urban.
workedExamples.answer: Southern Africa's population is proportionally about 2.4 times as urban as Eastern Africa's, the least urbanized region.

workedExamples.problem: Africa's urban population is now 41% of the total. By how many percentage points must it rise before the urban population exceeds the rural?
workedExamples.given: Current urban share = 41%; urban exceeds rural above 50%.
workedExamples.answer: At least 9 percentage points, which the textbook expects within about two decades.

commonMistakes: Confusing urbanization rate with population growth rate; urbanization is the share of people living in urban areas.
Assuming all of Africa is uniformly rural or uniformly urban when contrasts range from 12% to almost 90% urban.
Placing Ethiopia among the most urbanized countries, when it is listed in the bottom 10.
Naming Eastern Africa as the most urbanized region, when it is the least and Southern Africa is the most.
Thinking urban growth comes only from city birth rates and forgetting rural-urban migration.
Viewing urbanization as purely beneficial while ignoring strained services and rural depopulation.
applications: Explaining why Ethiopia's cities grow quickly while most of the country's people still live in rural areas.
Planning how a rapidly growing city should provide land, infrastructure, basic services and health care for new migrants.
Debating how rural depopulation weakens food crop production and raises poverty in the countryside.
Using the 2016 regional table to argue where investment in balanced rural development could slow distress migration.
Comparing Gabon's nearly 90% urban share with Burundi's 12% to show how uneven development paths are within Africa.
g10-geography-ug4-t5.summary: Urbanization in Africa is deeply uneven: Gabon is almost 90% urban while Burundi is least urbanized at 12%, and Eastern Africa (26% urban in 2016) trails Southern Africa (62%). About 41% of Africans live in urban areas today, a share expected to pass the rural population within about two decades. Rapid urban growth driven by rural migration strains land, infrastructure and health services, while uncontrolled urbanization depopulates rural areas, cripples food crop production and deepens poverty in both town and countryside.
